transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

I came in because I can’t shut my brain off anymore. One thing starts it—like a client not responding—and then within minutes I’m thinking I’ll lose the contract, fall behind on my divorce payments, and never get back into a real leadership role. It just keeps going.
How long has this pattern of worry and racing thoughts been going on—days, weeks, or longer?
It’s been going on since I was fired, about thirteen months ago. It never really eased up, even after I got the contract work.
Over these past thirteen months, have you also been feeling down, sad, or empty most of the day, nearly every day?
I’m not sure I’d call it sad or empty most of the day. I’m mostly just wound up and worried.
Along with the worry, have you noticed physical signs like muscle tension, feeling restless or on edge, or trouble concentrating on most days during this time?

Yeah, almost every day. I feel wound up most of the day—my shoulders are tight like I’m bracing for bad news. I’ll pace around the house or just bounce my leg during calls, even when nothing is actually going on.
Have you been having trouble falling asleep or staying asleep because your mind keeps racing with these worries?

Yeah. Most nights I’m lying there replaying interview answers or checking the clock at two or three in the morning. Even if I get what should be enough sleep, I wake up feeling like I was on call all night for a system outage.
When these worries start, do you find it hard to stop them or shift your focus away, even when you try?

Yeah, I can’t really stop it. It starts with one thing—like a client not getting back to me—and then within a few minutes I’m thinking I’ll lose the contract, fall behind on my divorce payments, and never get back into a real leadership role. I try to focus on something else, but my brain just keeps going.
Over these past 13 months, have you noticed yourself becoming more irritable or easily annoyed than usual?

Yeah, definitely. I’ve been snapping at people over stupid things—like a friend being late to soccer, or my family asking me a simple question. Afterwards I know I overreacted, but in the moment I just have no patience.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports 13 months of pervasive, difficult-to-control worry spanning multiple life domains (work, finances, career), accompanied by muscle tension, restlessness, sleep disturbance, irritability, and subjective difficulty concentrating due to racing thoughts. Symptoms are chronic (>6 months), present most days, and not better explained by a depressive episode (patient denies pervasive sadness/emptiness) or an adjustment disorder given the duration and diffuse worry content extending beyond the initial job loss stressor. This presentation meets criteria for Generalized Anxiety Disorder (F41.1).
